title: Maximising Transparency in Context Compaction Improves Retention of Facts and Commitments for Lightweight Coding Agents

Long coding agent sessions outgrow the model’s context window, so agents compact : older history is replaced by something shorter, usually a model-written summary. A summary selects and rewords, and the agent cannot see what was lost. Existing work has explored a range of compaction techniques, but comparatively little attention has been paid to their effectiveness with lightweight models, including those deployed locally or used for high-volume workloads. Here, we present transparent-compact, a simple deterministic method for the open-source Pi coding agent, designed specifically for use with such models and with the purpose of maximising the transparency of the agent’s view of its own compacted context. It guarantees that user and assistant prose in its context is unchanged by a model or algorithm, and explicitly flags where compaction has stripped information. We compare it with Pi’s default model-written summary and with pi-vcc, a popular deterministic compaction method with similar methods but without verbatim retention of prose. Our benchmarks run on four models of varying performance levels, with emphasis on Qwen3.8-27B: a lightweight model at the top end of what consumer hardware can serve locally. On sets probing commitments (rules the user set which exist only in the conversation) and recall of facts, transparent-compact matched or outperformed both alternatives. In particular, it showed an advantage in avoiding confident blunders, i.e. assertion of false information as opposed to recognizing that something was not recalled. Even with a frontier model, transparent-compact’s advantage was still present but smaller, suggesting that method is broadly effective, although the strongest models are able to compensate for ambiguous summaries more effectively. We argue that transparent-compact spares lightweight models from reasoning or searching their way around what compaction lost, and results in improved recall and application of critical information as a result, without the need for task or context-specific structuring of the session history.

A coding agent works in long sessions. It reads files, runs commands and tests, and talks with the user about what to do. Most of what fills its context is tool output: about 84% of an average SWE-agent turn [ 11 ] , and input tokens, not output tokens, drive the cost of agentic work [ 2 ] . When the context approaches the model’s window, the agent compacts . The usual approach is to ask the model to summarise the older history and continue from the summary [ 17 ] . A summary is selective by design. It keeps what the summariser judged important, in the summariser’s words, and nothing in the agent’s new context marks what was dropped or changed.

Some losses can be repaired, for example the agent can re-read a file or re-run a test. But other losses are silently damaging: A user’s commitments (“don’t touch the migration folder”, “no need for backwards compatibility”, “we agreed to keep it in one file”) may exist only in the conversation. If nothing in the repository reveals them, then an agent that has lost one can act against it without noticing. Recent work has shown that compaction silently erases such constraints: violations rose from 0% with the policy in context to 30% after compaction, and stayed at 0% when the constraint survived the summary [ 4 ] .

Compaction methods are typically developed against the most capable frontier models, whose capabilities allow them to compensate for some of the limitations of lossy summaries. This paper focuses instead on lighter weight models that are effective enough to have real-world utility, but whose weaker reasoning exposes them to failures deriving from compaction. A 27-billion-parameter model such as Qwen3.8-27B now runs on a single consumer GPU and can drive a coding agent. Such lightweight models are attractive for privacy, cost and offline use, but summary-based compaction serves them poorly in two ways. First, a model-written summary is slow and fragile on local hardware. Second, and more fundamentally, a lighter model is less able to compensate for a lossy summary: to notice what is missing, guess what an abbreviated line meant, and search its history persistently until it finds the original.
We propose that compaction for lightweight models should guarantee transparency in three senses:
What is kept in context is kept verbatim : the user’s and the agent’s own words are retained absolutely, not as a reinterpretation.
What is removed is explicitly declared , so the model knows what it no longer has.
All of what is removed is recoverable in one step , and recovery protocols and conditions are parsimonious and well defined.

transparent-compact [ 6 ] , which we built as an extension for the open-source Pi coding agent [ 22 ] , implements these properties ( Section 3.1 ). It removes tool outputs and reasoning, which make up most of the context and can be re-read or recovered, and keeps everything that was said by both the user and agent. The guiding principle is to aid the model in avoiding confabulation and false certainty: Summary and information compression invites misplaced certainty on partial information. Conversely, declaring what information is removed tells the agent which of its beliefs rest on material it no longer has, keeping the original words leaves no paraphrase to misread, and one-step recovery lets the agent check instead of guessing.

In this study we compared transparent-compact with Pi’s default model-written summary (pi-default) and with pi-vcc [ 14 ] , a widely used deterministic extractor for Pi that is functionally closer to transparent-compact, on two kinds of probe: commitments in real sessions, and facts planted in synthetic sessions and probed after repeated compaction. Transparency matters most for the kind of error that a lossy context invites. When information is missing and the agent knows it, the agent can look it up, check, or say that it does not know, and the user can step in: the failure is visible and cheap to repair. When the context instead holds something that only looks like the answer, such as a reworded rule, a stale value or a fragment of code, the agent acts on it with confidence, and the user has no reason to check. In a coding agent such confident errors turn directly into actions, such as a broken commitment or a wrong value written into a file. We therefore distinguish confident blunders separately from uncertain errors and reports of missing knowledge. The main model is Qwen3.8-27B running locally. Two other lightweight models (GPT-6 Luna and Gemma4 31B) and a frontier model (GPT-6.1 Sol) test how the results depend on the model. Scoring was blind to the method, and a replication package is available publically.
A method: transparent-compact, a minimal, deterministic, verbatim compaction scheme with delegated recovery over the raw session history, released as a Pi extension ( Section 3.1 ).

Evidence on two probe sets ( Figure 1 , Section 4 ). On commitments, transparent-compact led both alternatives on all three lightweight models, and pi-vcc’s failures were mostly confident. On planted facts it led pi-default by 22–42 points.

A mechanism ( Section 5.1 ). Both lossy methods select . Extraction cuts the qualifying clauses that carry a rule; rewriting keeps rules but narrows or reframes them, and every such error was confident. transparent-compact never lacked a commitment that another method kept.

Model dependence ( Section 5.2 ). How well lossy compaction works depends on how hard the model searches. The same pi-vcc context gave 98% recall on Qwen and 46% on Luna. transparent-compact held at 95–98% on both, and its advantage on commitments was smaller on the frontier model.

Keeping information outside a model’s context and retrieving it only when it is needed is not a new idea. Retrieval-augmented generation conditions a language model on passages fetched from an external store at inference time [ 10 ] , and agent frameworks have since applied the same principle to the agent’s own history and workspace. When a conversation exceeds the context window, an agent can summarise it, drop parts of it, or move it to external storage that the model queries on demand. MemGPT treats the context window as a small working memory backed by larger storage, with the model paging information in and out [ 15 ] . Anthropic’s guidance on context engineering describes compaction as summarising a conversation near the limit and restarting from the summary, and calls the clearing of old tool results “one of the safest lightest touch forms of compaction” [ 17 ] . Longer windows are only a partial substitute, since models use information in the middle of a long context less reliably than information near its ends [ 12 ] .

The closest relative of our method is observation masking . Lindenbauer et al. [11] compared LLM summarisation with masking, which replaces older tool outputs with a placeholder, on SWE-bench Verified. With Qwen3-Coder 480B, masking solved about as many instances as summarisation (54.8% against 53.8%), and both roughly halved the cost per instance relative to an agent without context management (reductions of 52.7% and 50.4%). transparent-compact extends masking in three ways: it masks the model’s reasoning as well as tool outputs, it survives repeated compaction by carrying forward the prose of every earlier span, and it makes everything it masks recoverable. Where that work measured end-task success, we measure what the agent still knows and acts on after compaction.

Compaction itself has recently been evaluated more directly. Factory compared three production compressors using probes for recall, artifacts, continuation and decisions, scored by an LLM judge, including over repeated compression [ 5 ] . TRACE evaluates single compaction events through paired continuations from the same environment state [ 13 ] . Closest to our commitment probes, Chen [4] showed that compaction erases in-context governance constraints, and proposed constraint pinning , which quarantines the constraints from lossy compaction. transparent-compact pins every user message by construction, so it needs no step that decides which lines are rules. Even without compaction, prohibitions decay under context pressure while requirements persist [ 7 ] .

Pi [ 22 ] is an open-source, extensible coding agent. Its default compaction asks the model for a structured summary with sections for the goal, “Constraints & Preferences”, progress, “Key Decisions”, next steps and critical context; later compactions update the previous summary. Extensions can replace compaction entirely.

pi-vcc [ 14 ] , inspired by the View-oriented Conversation Compiler [ 23 ] , builds its summary without model calls. It extracts the session goal, files and changes, commits, outstanding errors and user preferences into sections, keeps a brief transcript, and offers a search tool over the raw session for recovery. We chose pi-vcc as our main comparison because it is a widely used extension that closely resembles transparent-compact: both replace Pi’s compaction without any model calls, both produce checkpoints deterministically and both keep the full history recoverable through a search tool over the raw session. Their raw session recovery methods differ but have comparable costs in terms of time and output token usage. The key differences lie in what remains in the agent’s context, and how the full history is structured for retrieval. transparent-compact guarantees that text is either kept word for word or removed from the context entirely and replaced with a flag depending on type, whereas pi-vcc reduces the text algorithmically, extracting lines that match keywords and phrases into sections and truncating the rest to first lines, one-line turns and a capped transcript. Likewise, transparent-compact’s retrieval is comparatively straightforward, giving the subagent basic tools to scan the raw session file, whereas pi-vcc utilizes more post-hoc mechanisms for structuring and parsing the history.

Two other popular extensions differ in ways that make pi-vcc the cleaner comparison. pi-blackhole [ 9 ] builds on pi-vcc’s compaction code but adds an observational memory written by background model calls, so it would not isolate the compaction step. billion-context-pi [ 18 ] belongs to a different category, self-compression, in which the model decides what to compress by calling a tool.

At each compaction, transparent-compact replaces the older history with a checkpoint ( Section 3.1.3 ), and, as per Pi’s standard behaviour, keeps the most recent part of the conversation unchanged after it (its keepRecentTokens setting). For the span being compacted, the checkpoint keeps every user message and all assistant prose word for word. It reduces each tool call to a one-line signature, consisting of the tool name and truncated arguments, so that the agent knows what it did, and it lists the files read and modified, each marked as not in context. Tool outputs and the model’s reasoning are removed. Spans from earlier compactions are carried forward, so that after several compactions the checkpoint still holds everything that was said in the session.

The checkpoint also declares what it removed. Its header states what is kept and what is not, and that retained prose is “a record of what was said, not verification of its claims”. A short re-orient block follows. It asks the agent to re-read the documents its instructions require, to check the state of the repository before relying on it, to re-read any file before editing it, and to treat anything it knows only from removed reasoning or tool output as unverified until checked.

Pi’s session file is append-only, so everything that compaction removed remains on disk. transparent-compact exposes it through a single tool, context_lookup . The agent asks a question in natural language, and a subagent searches the full session history, including earlier reasoning and complete tool outputs, in its own context. It returns only the relevant findings, and labels those that rest on the model’s earlier reasoning. Three bounded fallback tools (list, grep and show entries) are available when the findings are incomplete, and consecutive lookups are capped. The delegation is deliberate: the main agent makes one call and receives an answer, instead of paging through search results itself. This reduces the risk of re-introducing excessive amounts of the removed history back into the compacted context.

As transparent-compact avoids compressing text, it is not possible to maintain its guarantees through an indefinite number of compactions. The conversation section of the checkpoint is capped, by default at 25% of the model’s window. With realistic usage, this allows for approximately 10 rounds of compaction before capping begins to apply. Once this upper bound of verbatim compactions is reached, conservative truncation begins to be applied similarly to pi-vcc, with similar behaviour expected at maximal truncation ( > 20 >20 rounds). Testing behaviour after large numbers of compactions is beyond the scope of this study.

We compare transparent-compact (v0.8.0), pi-vcc (v0.8.12, see Appendix A for discussion of different pi-vccversions), and pi-default(v1.1.0). In the pi-default condition the summaries are written by the same model that answers the probes. All methods run inside Pi with the same model, settings, prompts and session material.

Four models were used. Qwen3.8-27B [ 16 ] ( unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF , 6-bit quantisation, xhigh effort) and Gemma4 31B [ 21 ] ( unsloth/gemma-4-31B-it-GGUF , 5-bit quantisation, reasoning enabled) run locally on llama.cpp. Qwen runs at its highest reasoning setting with temperature 0.7, top- k k 20 and top- p p 0.95; Gemma uses its recommended sampling. GPT-6 Luna and GPT-6.1 Sol run through the OpenAI Codex provider at medium reasoning, which exposes no temperature or seed. We class Qwen, Gemma and Luna as lightweight models and Sol as a frontier model. transparent-compact’s lookup subagent always uses the same model as the agent.

Table 2 summarises the two probe sets. Commitment probes test whether the agent still honours what was settled in a real conversation. For each session, a fresh Claude Opus writer, briefed without any mention of compaction methods, identified commitments made early in the session: constraints (something the user required, forbade or waived) and decisions (a choice or convention that was agreed). For each commitment it wrote a natural next user message that would quietly break the commitment if the agent had forgotten it, without mentioning it. A separate Opus validator checked each probe against eight criteria. The commitment’s key strings had to appear exactly once in the session, so that nothing later restates it, and each probe has a control message that states the commitment; probes whose control failed were excluded, leaving 27 probes in 18 sessions.

Planted-fact probes test recall after repeated compaction. Eighteen synthetic debugging sessions, six stories with distinct plots each instantiated with three sets of values, are built to resemble real sessions, with about 85% of their tokens in tool output. Seventeen details are planted early in each session, among them codes seen once in a log, values that change twice, details that appear only in tool output or only in the model’s reasoning, and asides about hosts and people. Each session is compacted three times, each time at about 95k tokens, as for a 128k window, and after each compaction the agent answers questions on all planted details and on three lures. Every round opens with an episode that creates look-alikes of the planted values, so that a vague memory does not suffice.

The real sessions come from a public dataset of Pi sessions [ 1 ] , restricted to MIT or CC-BY-4.0 licences. Each session is replayed through each method’s actual compaction at a 48k-token window, so long sessions are compacted many times before the probe. No session text, probe text or model reply is published.

The agent must not reach what compaction removed except through its method’s own recovery tool. Probe turns therefore run on a copy of the compacted session with no file, shell or edit tools, and the only tool available is the method’s recovery tool ( context_lookup or vcc_recall ; pi-default has none). In the commitment study, an arm-neutral sentence tells the agent that it has no shell or file access in this turn. Probe turns declare a 128k window, so that they cannot trigger a further compaction.

Planted-fact answers are scored by rule, and a confident wrong answer is a wrong or superseded value that is not marked as unverified or unknown. Commitment replies are scored by blind Claude Sonnet judges, who see the commitment, the instruction, the pass criterion and the reply, but not the method, the session or the repetition. On commitment probes the judge also labels each failure as confident , meaning that the reply went ahead without any doubt, question or flag, or not. A second blind judge re-scored a seeded 25% of the replies in each run, with agreement between κ = 0.67 \kappa=0.67 and κ = 1.0 \kappa=1.0 .

The planted-fact and commitment studies are analysed with two-way repeated-measures ANOVAs with the factors model and method. For planted facts the subjects are the 18 sessions, which are identical on every model, and the outcome is each session’s recall over the three compactions, on Qwen, Luna and Gemma. For commitments the subjects are the 27 probes and the outcome is each probe’s pass rate over three repetitions, on all four models; failed turns, and the one probe whose session pi-default could not replay on Qwen, count as failures. The first commitment run, on Qwen, used five repetitions per probe. We found three repetitions enough to reduce the noise from the model’s sampling, and five excessive; because the runs were costly, all later runs used three, and the ANOVA uses repetitions one to three of the Qwen run. We apply Greenhouse–Geisser corrections and report partial η 2 \eta^{2} . To locate a method effect, we also fit the same ANOVA to each pair of methods, whose interaction term then tests whether that pair’s gap differs between models. Because the outcomes are bounded rates, the F F tests are approximate. The planted-fact study on Sol was added later with two methods only; it is reported as an exploratory update, analysed with a paired sign-flip permutation test over sessions, and is not part of the ANOVA. Non-significant differences are reported with their estimate and p p -value, as weak evidence in their direction rather than as evidence of no difference.

A replication package that re-runs the planted-fact and commitment studies with one’s own model, Pi installation and judge is available at https://github.com/felixwoolford/compaction-study-replication .
Figure 1 shows the three methods on both probe sets, and Table 3 gives the ANOVAs.

Across the four models, the compaction method had a reliable effect on how often the agent honoured a commitment ( F ⁡ ( 2 , 52 ) = 5.37 F(2,52)=5.37 , p = 0.008 p=0.008 , η p 2 = 0.17 \eta_{p}^{2}=0.17 ). The models also differed strongly in overall level ( F ⁡ ( 3 , 78 ) = 15.1 F(3,78)=15.1 , p < 0.001 p<0.001 ): Qwen and Sol passed most probes, Luna and Gemma far fewer ( Table 4 ). The model × \times method interaction was not significant ( F ⁡ ( 6,156 ) = 1.43 F(6,156)=1.43 , p = 0.22 p=0.22 ), so the ordering of the methods did not differ reliably between models.

The pairwise ANOVAs locate the method effect. transparent-compact outperformed pi-vcc ( F ⁡ ( 1 , 26 ) = 9.98 F(1,26)=9.98 , p = 0.004 p=0.004 , η p 2 = 0.28 \eta_{p}^{2}=0.28 ), and did so on every model: by 21 points on Qwen, 19 on Luna, 7 on Gemma and 11 on Sol, with no reliable difference in the size of the gap between models ( F ⁡ ( 3 , 78 ) = 1.35 F(3,78)=1.35 , p = 0.27 p=0.27 ). On Qwen, where five repetitions were run, comparison with pi-vcc gave 75.6% against 54.8% ( p = 0.001 p=0.001 ), and it held in every sensitivity analysis.

Against pi-default the difference was smaller and not significant overall ( F ⁡ ( 1 , 26 ) = 2.25 F(1,26)=2.25 , p = 0.15 p=0.15 , η p 2 = 0.08 \eta_{p}^{2}=0.08 ). Its pattern across models is nonetheless the one our argument predicts. transparent-compact was ahead on the three lightweight models, by 10 points on Qwen, 16 on Luna and 4 on Gemma, and behind by 5 on the frontier model, where Pi’s own summary had the highest pass rate of any condition (74.1% against 69.1%). The corresponding interaction did not reach significance ( F ⁡ ( 3 , 78 ) = 1.82 F(3,78)=1.82 , p = 0.16 p=0.16 ), so this is a pattern rather than a demonstrated interaction. pi-default in turn tended to outperform pi-vcc ( F ⁡ ( 1 , 26 ) = 3.28 F(1,26)=3.28 , p = 0.08 p=0.08 ).

How the agent failed matters as much as how often. A commitment broken without any sign of doubt gives the user no reason to check, whereas a reply that raises a question or flags a conflict does. Figure 2 divides every probe repetition into passes, failures that flagged doubt and confident failures. With pi-vcc, between a third and over half of all replies broke the commitment confidently (41% on Qwen, 52% on Luna, 56% on Gemma and 33% on Sol), against 15–37% with transparent-compact. Pi’s summary fell between the two on the lightweight models and matched transparent-compact on Sol. In the per-model tests, transparent-compact produced fewer confident failures than pi-vcc on Qwen ( p < 0.001 p<0.001 ) and Luna ( p = 0.008 p=0.008 ), with the same direction on Gemma ( p = 0.052 p=0.052 ) and Sol ( p = 0.12 p=0.12 ).

Gemma passed the fewest probes with every method. It rarely used its recovery tools: with transparent-compact it made a lookup in 12 of 79 turns, and on one probe it repeated identical searches until the turn timed out.

transparent-compact recalled more planted facts than Pi’s default summary on every model ( Table 5 ): 97.8% against 75.3% on Qwen, 95.1% against 55.0% on Luna and 93.3% against 51.5% on Gemma. This is the largest and most consistent effect in the study ( F ⁡ ( 1 , 17 ) = 860.2 F(1,17)=860.2 , p < 0.001 p<0.001 , η p 2 = 0.98 \eta_{p}^{2}=0.98 in the pairwise ANOVA). transparent-compact also gave fewer confident wrong answers than pi-default on all three models, by 3.5 points on Qwen, 5.4 on Luna and 4.4 on Gemma (Holm-corrected p ≤ 0.006 p\leq 0.006 in each case). The gap in recall was 22.5 points on Qwen and nearly twice that on Luna (40.1) and Gemma (41.7), so the pair’s interaction with the model was significant as well ( F ⁡ ( 2 , 34 ) = 42.1 F(2,34)=42.1 , p < 0.001 p<0.001 ).

pi-vcc behaved differently. It matched transparent-compact on Qwen (98.2% against 97.8%) but fell to 46% on Luna and 68% on Gemma, where its recall declined with each compaction (73.5%, 69.0% and 60.5%). transparent-compact’s recall, by contrast, held between 93% and 98% on all three models. The strong model × \times method interaction of the omnibus ANOVA ( Table 3 : F ⁡ ( 4 , 68 ) = 62.0 F(4,68)=62.0 , p < 0.001 p<0.001 ) therefore reflects how the two lossy methods fared on each model rather than any change in transparent-compact; Section 5.2 traces pi-vcc’s part of it to how persistently each model searched.

As an exploratory update, the planted-fact study was later also run on the frontier model, Sol, with transparent-compact and pi-default only ( Table 5 ). transparent-compact recalled 99.3% against 75.6% for Pi’s summary, more in all 18 sessions ( + 23.7 +23.7 points [20.6, 26.9], p < 0.001 p<0.001 ), and gave no confident wrong answers, against 2.1% for pi-default ( p = 0.002 p=0.002 ). Pi’s summary thus lost about as much on the frontier model as on Qwen (75.6% against 75.3%), although on Sol most of its losses were abstentions: of its 918 answers, 190 were “unknown” and 34 were wrong.

Twelve of the Qwen sessions were continued to eight compactions. transparent-compact’s recall stayed between 96.6% and 100% in every round, whereas Pi’s summary failed in most sessions at the fifth or sixth compaction, when the growing summary hit its generation cap. Over rounds four to eight, transparent-compact gave 6.5 points fewer confident wrong answers ( p = 0.006 p=0.006 ).

With Qwen, transparent-compact took 0.43 s per compaction and pi-vcc 0.40 s, whereas pi-default took 167.8 s because the local model writes the summary with full reasoning. Sol’s summaries took about 61 s each for pi-default.

transparent-compact’s context is larger, and its lookups add tokens ( Table 6 ). On Qwen’s commitment probes, its probe turns processed on average 57,300 prompt tokens that were not served from the cache, against 21,389 for pi-vcc (2.7 times as many); on Gemma the ratio was 1.7. Output tokens were similar. In the planted-fact sessions, where every probe turn required a lookup, transparent-compact’s sessions took about three minutes longer in total than those of pi-default despite its near-instant compaction (14.1 against 11.2 minutes, p = 0.077 p=0.077 ), and had no significant difference in duration compared to pi-vcc ( p = 0.78 p=0.78 ). It should be noted that as these sessions were entirely based on recalling information from earliest in the interaction, agents performed significantly more context retrievals than usual, and thus retrieval time dominated total session time in a way that would not be expected in practical use.

A model-written summary can also fail outright. At Pi’s stock settings for a 48k window, the summary may use 0.8 times the 8,192-token reserve, or 6,553 tokens; Qwen at its highest reasoning setting spent that budget thinking, and compaction failed in 15 of 16 real sessions. To allow for comparison with the other methods, we allowed a larger summary budget of the planted-fact study (26,214 tokens). Subsequently, 202 of 205 compactions succeeded, but 3 of 41 long sessions still failed after 7–9 compactions, when the repeatedly updated summary outgrew the budget. All pi-default results on Qwen in this paper use the larger budget, which favours pi-default relative to its stock behaviour. The summaries written by Luna, Gemma and Sol did not fail. Deterministic compaction cannot fail in this way.

The two clearest method effects run in opposite directions for the two alternatives. Pi’s summary fell far behind transparent-compact on planted facts but not significantly on commitments, whereas pi-vcc fell behind it on commitments but matched it on planted facts when the model searched persistently. Failure analyses of both studies, summarised in this section, trace each pattern to what the method chooses to keep. Both analyses are exploratory. The planted-fact analysis uses all 18 Qwen sessions for recall by source and the 12 sessions continued past three compactions for the review of confusions; the commitment analysis covers every Qwen probe under all three methods (26 probes × \times 3 repetitions × \times 3 methods).

A model-written summary keeps what the user said and compresses the rest. On Qwen’s planted facts, pi-default recalled 97.9% of the details the user had stated, 80.2% of those in assistant prose, 62.7% of those seen only in tool output and 15.8% of those that existed only in the model’s reasoning. Because pi-default has no recovery tool, whatever the summary omits is lost for good. transparent-compact removes tool outputs and reasoning from the context as well, but its agent recovered them through context_lookup and reached 100%, 100%, 97.6% and 87.4% for the same four sources. The lookup was used in every probe turn, because the questions were built to require recovery, so this rate does not reflect ordinary use.

paragraphs.en: Omission is not the only failure. In each of the 7 cases in which a detail was first answered correctly and later answered confidently wrong, the correct value was still in the summary. In 5 of them a competing value from a later look-alike episode stood beside it, and the context that had separated the two was gone. In one session, for example, the summary recorded that a backfill job’s batch size had been changed to 7,500 after benchmarks; after a later episode about a different job it also recorded “Chose 2750 because it runs clean”, no longer saying which job that referred to, and the agent then gave 2,750 as the agreed batch size. One summary also silently rewrote the day of a release freeze, an error the probes did not score, so they understate summary errors. The synthetic sessions were built to contain such look-alikes, so the rate of confusion reflects the material, but the mechanism does not: a summary can keep a value while losing the context that binds it to its episode, whereas transparent-compact keeps the original messages in which that context lives.

paragraphs.en: Table 7 shows where each commitment stood in each method’s context. pi-vcc has no reliable place for rules. Its only rule-like section, “User Preferences”, is filled by English-only patterns such as “prefer …” and “never use …”, and it appeared in only 1 of 15 summaries, with an irrelevant line. Its other sections truncate: the goal section keeps the first line of recent user messages, earlier turns are cut to one short line each, and the transcript excerpt keeps only its last 120 lines. These cuts often fell just before the qualifying clause that carried the constraint, and procedural rules survived only as traces of what had been done (a wait call, a worktree removal) rather than as the rule behind them. Language was not the main cause: 11 of the 15 sessions were mainly in English, and pi-vcc’s pass rate was about the same in those sessions (53%) as in the others (50%).

paragraphs.en: pi-vcc did search its history, calling its recall tool in 64 of 78 runs, and 30 of its 37 failures came after a search. The searches, however, looked for code to act on rather than for what had been agreed, and the retrieved code made the replies concrete and therefore confident: 19 of its 33 confident failures opened by saying that the exact code had been found in the history. Recovery by search works when the model knows what to look for, as with a planted fact named in the question; it does not help when the model does not know that a rule exists.

paragraphs.en: Pi’s summary template, by contrast, requires “Constraints & Preferences” and “Key Decisions” sections, and Qwen filled them with the user’s rules, often quoting them. Where a rule was present, pi-default passed 31 of 39 times, with one confident failure. This is why it came close to transparent-compact on commitments while falling far behind it on planted facts: the template keeps rules and decisions and compresses details such as values and outputs. Its commitment failures came from rewording rather than omission, since no pi-default failure lost a commitment that another method’s context kept. Instead the summary narrowed a rule’s scope, recorded a standing rule as a fact about one past task, kept a decision from before the user reversed it, or recorded a rule only as a past change, and all nine such failures were confident. How well a summary keeps rules depends on the model that writes it, which is consistent with Sol’s summaries giving the best commitment result of any condition ( Section 4.1 ).
paragraphs.zh: 相比之下，Pi 的摘要模板需要“约束与偏好”和“关键决策”部分，而 Qwen 则用用户的规则填充了这些部分，并经常直接引用这些规则。 在有规则存在的情况下，pi-default 在 39 次中有 31 次通过，仅有一次出现自信的失败。 这就是为什么它在承诺方面接近 transparent-compact，但在植入事实方面却远远落后：该模板保留了规则和决策，同时压缩了价值观和输出等细节。 其承诺失败源于措辞的改写而非遗漏，因为没有任何 pi-default 的失败会丢失其他方法在上下文中保留的承诺。 相反，摘要缩小了规则的适用范围，将一条长期有效的规则记录为关于某项过往任务的事实，保留了用户在撤销前已做出的决策，或仅将规则记录为过去的变更，而这九次失败均为自信判断。 摘要在多大程度上能保留规则取决于生成摘要的模型，这与 Sol 的摘要在所有条件下都取得了最佳承诺结果的情况一致（第 4.1 节）。

paragraphs.en: Both lossy methods select , and each selection rule has a blind spot ( Table 8 ). Rewriting selects by the summariser’s judgement. Pi’s template asks for rules and decisions, so it keeps them, but it compresses the values, outputs and reasoning that planted-fact questions ask for, and loses the context that tells look-alike values apart; without a recovery tool, nothing it drops can be restored. paragraphs.en: Each alternative is therefore competitive where its selection rule anticipates what is needed and falls behind where it does not, and the ANOVAs show exactly this. transparent-compact’s significant advantages are over Pi’s summary on planted facts ( F ⁡ ( 1 , 17 ) = 860.2 F(1,17)=860.2 , p < 0.001 p<0.001 ) and over pi-vcc on commitments ( F ⁡ ( 1 , 26 ) = 9.98 F(1,26)=9.98 , p = 0.004 p=0.004 ). Conversely, Pi’s summary came within a non-significant margin of transparent-compact on commitments, and pi-vcc matched it on planted facts with Qwen. transparent-compact does not select what was said, and makes everything else recoverable in one delegated step, so it has no comparable blind spot: it is the only one of the three methods that did not fall significantly behind another method on any probe set. Since an agent cannot know in advance which kind of information a later turn will depend on, this robustness across kinds of information, rather than a win on any single probe set, is the main advantage of the method. It matters most for lightweight models, which are least able to reason or search their way around a blind spot ( Section 5.2 ).

paragraphs.en: First, how well lossy compaction works depends on how hard the model searches. pi-vcc gives an identical compacted context to every model on the planted-fact material, because its compaction is deterministic and the material is the same, yet its recall was 98% on Qwen, 46% on Luna and 68% on Gemma. Luna made 5–14 calls per batch and then answered “unknown”: 401 of its 918 planted-fact answers with pi-vcc were abstentions, against 4 for Qwen. The tool worked in both cases; what differed was how persistently the model used it. transparent-compact’s lookup is a single delegated call, and its recall held between 93% and 98% on all three models.

paragraphs.en: The account in Section 5.1.4 points to a design principle rather than a tuning problem. Any rule for choosing what to keep encodes a guess about what later turns will need, and we expect a better template or a better extractor to move the blind spot rather than remove it (See Appendix A for an illustration of this in practice.). Commitments are a telling case: they are short, easy to miss, expressed in ordinary language rather than in any fixed form, and invisible in the environment. Chen [4] found the same with compaction and safety policies: violations were 0% when the constraint survived the summary and 38% when it was dropped. Their remedy, pinning the constraints, requires knowing which lines are constraints. transparent-compact keeps everything that was said, so nothing depends on recognising a rule, in any language. The cost of not selecting is a larger checkpoint, but because tool output dominates real sessions that cost is moderate: in our real sessions the median checkpoint (31k characters) was smaller than Pi’s summary (34k).

paragraphs.en: The pattern has a long history in the psychology of memory. People quickly lose the exact wording of what they hear but keep its meaning [ 20 ] . Fuzzy-trace theory holds that a verbatim trace and a gist trace are stored in parallel, that the verbatim trace fades faster, and that gist-based memories support confident false recognition [ 19 ] . Bartlett showed that remembering is reconstructive, bending material toward the rememberer’s schema [ 3 ] , and people often misattribute the source of a memory [ 8 ] . A model-written summary is a gist trace produced on purpose. The failures of pi-default resemble schema-driven reconstruction: rules were narrowed, or turned into facts about one past event, to fit the categories of a template, and every such failure was confident. transparent-compact keeps the verbatim trace together with its source, recording who said what, and labels what came from the agent’s own earlier reasoning as unverified. We offer this as an analogy that may guide design, not as evidence about how models work internally.

paragraphs.en: For practitioners, transparent-compact particularly suits local and lightweight models, and sessions in which users state rules and preferences. It is also at least as good with the tested frontier model as the other methods, and avoids slow model-written compaction, but further testing would be required to endorse adoption exclusively for use with frontier models. pi-vcc uses fewer prompt tokens per turn and recalls facts as well as transparent-compact when the model searches persistently. Pi’s default summary kept commitments best with the frontier model and reasonably well with Qwen, but it loses detail and, with weaker models, distorts rules confidently. Although the benchmarks for commitments use real session data, the probes do not necessarily reflect real world usage of agents, and pi-vcc’s maturity may make it more suitable in an applied setting. Nevertheless lthough the benchmark performance and simplicity of transparent-compact invite further development of this method as an applied tool, and adoption of its principles.
paragraphs.zh: 对于实践者而言，transparent-compact 尤其适合本地轻量模型，以及用户声明规则和偏好的会话。 在测试的前沿模型上，其表现至少与其他方法相当，并且避免了由模型编写的缓慢压缩过程；但若要完全采用它用于前沿模型，还需要进一步测试。pi-vcc 每轮使用的提示词更少，并且在模型持续搜索时能像 transparent-compact 一样准确回忆事实。 在前沿模型上，Pi 的默认摘要最能保持承诺，在 Qwen 上的表现也较为合理；但在较弱模型上，它会丢失细节，并可能自信地扭曲规则。 尽管承诺相关的基准测试使用了真实的会话数据，但这些探针并不一定反映智能体在现实世界中的使用方式；pi-vcc 的成熟度可能使其在实际应用中更为适用。 尽管如此，transparent-compact 在基准测试中的表现和简洁性，仍促使人们进一步将其发展为实用工具，并采纳其原则。

paragraphs.en: Compaction decides what a coding agent still knows. We compared three ways of compacting with four models, three of them lightweight. Keeping everything that was said word for word, dropping the bulky tool output and making the rest recoverable in one step was the only approach without a blind spot. It recalled far more planted facts than Pi’s model-written summary on every model, kept the user’s commitments better than pi-vcc’s extraction on every model, and did not fall significantly behind either alternative on any probe set. Each alternative fell behind where its rule for choosing what to keep failed to anticipate what was needed. Its lead over Pi’s summary on commitments was confined to the lightweight models, and on the frontier model Pi’s own summary did slightly better, though not significantly. This is consistent with our argument: simple, transparent compaction removes the need for the model to reason or search its way around what compaction lost, and lightweight models are the ones that most need that help.
paragraphs.zh: 压缩决定了编码智能体仍然知道哪些信息。 我们将三种压缩方法与四种模型进行了比较，其中三种是轻量级模型。 逐字保留所有已述内容、删除冗余的工具输出，并在一部操作中使其余内容可恢复，是唯一没有盲点的方法。 它在每个模型上都回忆出了比 Pi 的模型生成摘要多得多的植入事实，在每个模型上都比 pi-vcc 的提取方法更好地保留了用户的承诺，并且在任何探测集上都没有明显落后于其他两种方法。 每种替代方法都在其保留信息的规则未能预测到所需内容时出现了不足。 它在承诺保留方面相对于 Pi 摘要的优势仅限于轻量级模型；而在前沿模型上，Pi 自己的摘要表现略好一些，但差异并不显著。 这与我们的论点一致：简单透明的压缩消除了模型需要围绕压缩所丢失的内容进行推理或搜索的必要性，而轻量级模型正是最需要这种帮助的一类模型。

paragraphs.en: There are two popular and actively maintained versions of pi-vcc in the Pi package catalogue. @sting8k/pi-vcc is the original, and @monotykamary/pi-vcc forked from it in May 2026. The two versions still maintain the same compaction core, and primarily differ in their retrieval processes. Neither is simply a superset of the other.
paragraphs.zh: Pi 软件包目录中有两个广受欢迎且正在积极维护的 pi-vcc 版本。@sting8k/pi-vcc 是原始版本，而 @monotykamary/pi-vcc 则于 2026 年 5 月从中分叉而来。 这两个版本仍然保持着相同的压缩核心，主要区别在于它们的检索流程。 两者之间不存在简单的包含关系。

paragraphs.en: Preliminary testing indicated that @sting8k’s more complex retrieval often caused agents to make excessive retrieval calls while looking for specific information in our benchmarks – often hitting a 30 minute timeout for individual probes, especially in the planted facts study. We determined that the relative simplicity of @monotykamary’s retrieval made it a more suitable comparison for isolating different compaction principles of pi-vcc vs transparent-compact. In practical usage however, @sting8k is the more mature and popular version, and it appears likely that is the more performant version. Figure 4 shows results of exploratory analysis indicating that performance in the benchmark does differ between the two versions, especially with the Luna model, but the transparent-compact method still maintains an edge in these studies.
paragraphs.zh: 初步测试表明，在我们的基准测试中，@sting8k 更复杂的检索方式常常导致智能体在查找特定信息时发起过多的检索调用——尤其是在植入事实的研究中，单次查询经常达到 30 分钟的时间限制。 我们确定，@monotykamary 的检索方式相对简单，因此更适合用于区分 pi-vcc 和 transparent-compact 的不同压缩原理。 然而在实际应用中，@sting8k 是更成熟且更受欢迎的版本，并且很可能也是性能更强的版本。 图 4 展示了探索性分析的结果，表明两种版本在基准测试中的表现确实存在差异，尤其是在 Luna 模型上，但 transparent-compact 方法在这些研究中仍然保持优势。
